extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, historians of science, and advanced students interested in cultural evolution and the analogy between biological evolution and scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual framework for treating scientific knowledge/practice as a cultural Darwinian population and for assessing when scientific practices can evolve by natural selection. Emphasizes the components and mechanisms that make practices susceptible to directional (adaptive) change and the mechanisms by which practices are copied and persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal definition of a Darwinian population
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of causally connected individual things in which there is variation in character, which leads to differences in reproductive output, and which is inherited to some extent (Godfrey‑Smith 2009, 39).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this minimal set of conditions (variation, differential reproductive output, and some inheritance) as the baseline test for whether a set of items (e.g., practices, ideas, habits) can be treated as a population subject to evolutionary analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heredity (H)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which offspring resemble parents, due to the causal role of parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how strongly instances of a practice reproduce their parents' features; high heredity means practices are copied with high fidelity across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsicality (S)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which differences in reproductive output in a population depend on intrinsic features of the members of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether certain practices succeed because of their own properties (intrinsic advantages) rather than solely because of external factors; high intrinsicality means selection can act on those intrinsic differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity (C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the magnitude of trait differences tracks the magnitude of their fitness differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether small differences between practices correspond to small differences in reproductive success (and large differences to large fitness differences); continuity lets selection refine traits gradually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigmatic Darwinian population (high H, S, C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Populations that are ripe for evolution by natural selection are those that exhibit high heredity, high intrinsicality, and high continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat H, S, and C jointly: only when all three are sufficiently strong will adaptive, directional refinement (analogue of biological adaptation) plausibly operate on practices or cultural items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practices as heritable units
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices reproduce by causing more instances of themselves (e.g., a lawn‑mowing style that neighbors adopt from observing you).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether something (concept, technique, problem) can be part of a Darwinian analysis, determine if it can behave as a discrete, reproducible unit that spawns further instances via causal transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for practices to count as Darwinian (three practice conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A population of practices is paradigmatic Darwinian whenever: (1) Practices reproduce with high fidelity; (2) Differences in practices' reproductive success depend on intrinsic features of the practices themselves; (3) The magnitude of differences between practices tracks the magnitude of their fitness differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three conditions directly when judging whether scientific practices will be refined by natural‑selection‑like processes; each condition maps to H, S, and C respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for high-fidelity copying for directional refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: A high degree of resemblance between parents and offspring is required for populations to share the same selective environment and therefore for directional selection to operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the pedagogical and cultural mechanisms in a community produce sufficiently faithful transmission of practices; without high‑fidelity copying, vertical (deepening) progress is undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive value of copying depends on distance from optimum and environment stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The adaptive value of high‑fidelity copying depends on (1) a trait's distance from a phenotypic optimum and (2) the stability of the environment: perfect copying is favored at the optimum and in stable environments; imperfect copying is favored when traits are suboptimal or environments change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to judge when conservatism versus variation is epistemically beneficial: in stable domains near an optimum, enforce strong copying; in changing or exploratory contexts, allow more variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of environmental stabilization over variation suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: When a trait is optimized, there will be pressure to both suppress variation and stabilize the environment; of these, pressure to stabilize the environment must be primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether communities attempt to shape/stabilize problem environments (e.g., canonical problems, standards) as a prerequisite to successful refinement, rather than merely suppressing variation among practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework can represent nonadaptive evolutionary change
rubrics_metrics.description: By setting the heredity, intrinsicality, and continuity 'dials' to different points on a continuum, the Darwinian populations framework can represent evolutionary phenomena that are epistemically significant and evolutionary but not easily understood in terms of increasing adaptedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume selection is always dominant; use the H/S/C parameters to model cases where selection is weak or other nonselective mechanisms drive change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural evolution emphasizes individual learning (weakens selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevalence of individual learning in cultural evolution tends to weaken the influence of selection; nonselective change due to individual learning is likely more significant in cultural evolution than nonselective processes in genetic evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating cultural practices, account for individual learning and other nonselective transmission mechanisms that can swamp or alter selection's effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific consensus as allelic fixation ('consensus practice')
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific consensus is the analogue of allelic fixation: the group of practices that have gone to fixation are 'consensus practice.' Consensus reduces variation and promotes high‑fidelity copying by inertia, but consensus typically must be maintained by selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence or absence of consensus as an indicator of how readily practices will be copied across generations and of a community's propensity for directional refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of inheritance/transmission in science: undergraduate curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Undergraduate curricula transmit general forms and substances of research problems (families of problems), laying foundations for later inheritance of specific problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate curricula as a scaffold that orients novices to legitimate problem types; strong curricular transmission increases resemblance in problem framing across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of inheritance: specialized formal training
rubrics_metrics.description: Advanced formal training has a narrow range of application; students trained in specialized formal approaches tend to continue working on problems to which those approaches apply, thereby perpetuating problem types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how specialized methodological training channels future research agendas and thus acts as selective pressure to reproduce particular problem types and approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of inheritance: experimental training and model systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate students/postdocs acquire extensive experience with particular technologies or model organisms, which limits exportability and promotes continued use of familiar problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring fidelity of practice copying, include the degree to which laboratory techniques, model systems, and hands‑on skills constrain or direct future research choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of inheritance: assignment of research problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct assignment of research problems to trainees is a relatively strong mechanism by which research problems are inherited in the natural sciences; trainees often have little control over their dissertation problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the degree of top‑down problem assignment in a discipline as a predictor of high‑fidelity transmission of problem agendas across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization and progenation of scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: Training and professionalization (graduate education, mentoring, research groups) produce new practitioners who carry forward existing research problems and problem‑solving practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional structures (labs, mentorship models, professional incentives) for how effectively they reproduce community practices and thereby sustain particular research programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of phylogenetic/statistical methods for cultural practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When practices can be treated as 'discrete heritable units' (e.g., words, possibly concepts), phylogenetic and statistical tools can model their history (Pagel's program); this is an exemplar for applying evolutionary methods to scientific concepts/practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the target practices/concepts are discrete and trackable enough to support phylogenetic analysis; if so, such methods can illuminate descent and selective pressures, but conceptual histories must meet data and discreteness requirements.
